title: Boston’s Fusion Food Is Better, and More Personal, Than Ever
summary: The ’90s gave fusion cooking a bad name. Boston chefs are taking it back. The post Boston’s Fusion Food Is Better, and More Personal, Than Ever appeared first on Boston Magazine .
content: This story is part of a series on dining trends that appeared in the November 2026 print issue as part of the Top 50 Restaurants feature . Phat Thaiger’s khao soi maki. / Photo by Rachel Leah Blumenthal At first glance, the khao soi maki at Phat Thaiger in Malden seems like a familiar sushi roll: hamachi and avocado wrapped in seaweed and rice. Then northern Thailand crashes the party. Sliced red onions and crispy noodles pile on top, while a creamy yellow curry sauce pulls the whole thing in a completely different direction. It sounds strange, yet somehow it all makes perfect sense. It’s easily one of the tastiest bites in Greater Boston right now—just don’t call it “Asian fusion.” The phrase still carries the baggage of the 1990s , when fusion became shorthand for chefs mashing cuisines together because, well, they could. What’s happening around Boston now is something else: wildly creative, highly personal cooking with stories that started long before these restaurants did. Fusion food has gone in and out of style, and the gimmicky ’90s didn’t do the term any favors. But people have been cooking this way for centuries, wherever cultures have crossed paths through trade, migration, colonization, or shifting borders. Nobody, for instance, calls gumbo “fusion,” though its West African, French, Spanish, and Native American roots make it exactly that. “There has been fusion before any of us were alive,” says Tracy Chang , chef-owner of Pagu in Cambridge, a restaurant with Spanish, Japanese, and Taiwanese influences. “There has been fusion before social media. There has been fusion before Escoffier wrote his book [ Le Guide Culinaire ], before Harold McGee wrote his book [ On Food and Cooking ]. It just hasn’t really been documented as such; maybe they weren’t using that word. Migration patterns dictate how cuisines evolve.” Around Greater Boston today, those influences often come straight from the chefs’ own lives. Take Lê Madeline in Quincy , where restaurateur Tam Le and executive chef Peter Nguyen blend traditional Vietnamese cuisine with influences from their Vietnamese-American childhoods, plus Nguyen’s experiences working in Texas and beyond. You could call it fusion. Nguyen prefers “Vietnamese reimagined,” adding, “Yes, I’m fusing foods, but I’m keeping Vietnamese food at the root.” Curried edamame, gyoza, and more at Mimi’s Chūka Diner. / Photo by Rachel Leah Blumenthal At Mimi’s Chūka Diner , the fusion comes from two very different family histories. The restaurant melds chūka cuisine—itself a Japanese take on Chinese food—with the American diner. Cofounders Ted Woo and Jon Awerman met working at B & G Oysters more than a decade ago. Woo is “mostly Chinese but with a little bit of Japanese heritage,” as he explained shortly before Mimi’s opening. His mother grew up in Japan, where his uncles ran Chinese restaurants. Awerman’s grandparents owned New York City diners. The dinner menu at Mimi’s is mostly chūka at the moment—although Woo teases changes to come—but the chūka -diner fusion comes out to play at brunch, with dishes like dou miao (pea shoot) Benedict. Of course, some fusion traditions long ago became cuisines of their very own: For instance, Nikkei, or Peruvian-Japanese cooking (see Nōhri in Chinatown and Ruka downtown), and chifa , or Peruvian-Chinese cooking (see La Royal in Cambridge and Peruvian Taste in Charlestown). At Pagu, meanwhile, all that history gets personal. Chang’s restaurant grew out of what she ate growing up, where she later worked, and the foods she came to love. “This is how I cook at home,” she says. “If you come over, I might make [this cuisine] for you.” It starts with the Japanese and Taiwanese dishes she ate as a child. Chang’s grandmother grew up in Taiwan eating Japanese food during the island’s half-century under Japanese colonial rule; in her sixties, she came here and opened a Japanese restaurant. Later, Chang worked at Martín Berasategui’s eponymous three-star Michelin restaurant in San Sebastian, Spain (Basque Country), fueling a love of Basque and Spanish cuisines. Still, the baggage of past iterations of fusion makes chefs wary of the f-word. But increasingly, they’re willing to own it. “It’s an ‘If you can’t beat ’em, join ’em’ sort of a moment,” says Woo, noting that the term “fusion food” used to have “a negative connotation in my mind, something that put a cuisine or restaurant into a box”—things like Philly cheesesteak eggrolls and Chinese chicken salads. At first, he says, he hoped to avoid the “Asian fusion” label for Mimi’s, “given the perceived hokeyness of the genre. [But] as chefs continue to create food that bridges multiple cuisines or techniques with meaningful origin stories, the term ‘fusion’ can also adopt the definition ‘unique to the chef.’” Besides, says Woo, “diners have more open minds these days about what fusion food is and can be. Or is it because the ’90s are cool again?” Lê Madeline’s Việt Cajun crawfish noodles: garlic noodles, basil-buttered crawfish, parmesan, salmon roe. / Photo by Rachel Leah Blumenthal The 1990s, sure, but also the 1890s. And the 1790s. Cuisines travel with people, change in their new homes, and change again with the next generation. Maybe that’s what separates today’s most interesting fusion cooking from the gimmicks of decades past: There’s a reason—or centuries of reasons—why those ingredients ended up on the same plate. “There’s a purpose to why I’m doing this,” says Lê Madeline’s Nguyen, of his New England and Texas-accented Vietnamese cuisine. “It’s gotta be a good story.” This story first appeared in the print edition of the November 2026 issue with the headline “The New Fusion.” Related News Why Are Massachusetts Tipping Laws So Hard to Understand?
